props.title: The New York Ripper

sections.content: The New York Ripper represents Lucio Fulci's most controversial and brutal giallo, pushing slasher conventions into extreme territory. The film follows a killer with a bizarre duck voice terrorizing New York City, featuring graphic murder sequences that caused the film to be banned in the UK. While Maniac (1980) and Dressed to Kill (1980) explored similar themes of urban decay and sexual violence in New York, Fulci's approach is deliberately more transgressive, combining giallo's stylized murder set-pieces with an unflinching depiction of Times Square's seedy underbelly.

sections.content: The film's placement in Fulci's career marks a significant shift from his earlier supernatural works like City of the Living Dead (1980) and The Beyond (1981). While those films explored metaphysical horror, The New York Ripper grounds itself in urban decay and sexual psychosis. Its cynical worldview and extreme violence align more closely with American slashers like Ms. 45 (1981) and Maniac (1980), while maintaining giallo's signature stylized murder sequences and complex mystery plotting.

The film's treatment of gender and sexuality remains deeply problematic, even by exploitation film standards. Unlike more nuanced contemporary works like Dressed to Kill (1980) or Windows (1980), Fulci's approach lacks any pretense of social commentary. However, the film's technical elements - from Giuseppe Pinori's neon-drenched cinematography to Francesco De Masi's pulsing score - demonstrate the high production values typical of Italian genre cinema of the period. sections.content: While initially dismissed as pure exploitation, The New York Ripper has gained reappraisal as a bridge between Italian giallo and American slasher traditions. Its influence can be seen in later urban horror films like Maniac Cop (1988) and William Lustig's other New York-set horror films. The film's unflinching depiction of violence presaged the extreme cinema movement of the 2000s, though works like Inside (2007) and Martyrs (2008) would approach similar themes with more artistic ambition.
